```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(pdmS7)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  error = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 4.2, dpi = if (nzchar(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"))) 110 else 60
)
logger::log_threshold(logger::WARN, namespace = "pdmS7")
```

The PDM stays as published. What can still be improved is everything around it: what the
calibration counts as a good fit, which parameters it bothers to fit, how a model is judged,
whether it holds when the climate shifts, and how sure we are of it. This article takes each in
turn on one made-up catchment, so every answer can be checked against the truth.

```{r data}
rain <- synthetic_rain("2017-10-01", years = 3, dt = 1, seed = 5)
truth <- modifyList(pdm_presets("standard"), list(area_km2 = 25))
model <- pdm_from_config(truth)
forcing <- rain[c("time", "rain", "pet")]
set.seed(8)
flow <- run_pdm(model, forcing[c("rain", "pet")], initial_state(model, 0.5))$output$q_m3s
observed <- flow * exp(rnorm(length(flow), 0, 0.15))   # a gauge's error grows with the flow
start <- modifyList(truth, list(fc = 0.8))
start$distribution$cmax <- 200
lower <- c(fc = 0.6, distribution.cmax = 100, surface.k1 = 1, distribution.b = 0.1)
upper <- c(fc = 1.4, distribution.cmax = 500, surface.k1 = 30, distribution.b = 2)
```

# 1. Count every error fairly

A gauge's error at a flood is many times its error at baseflow, and so is a model's. NSE squares
the raw errors, so the few largest floods outweigh the rest of the record: the calibration
effectively fits a handful of peaks. Box-Cox transformed flows (`boxcox_flow()`) shrink the big
flows more than the small ones, until the errors are about the same size at every flow, which
is what least squares assumes. `objective = "boxcox"` scores 1 - NSE on that scale.

```{r boxcox}
fit_nse <- calibrate_pdm(start, forcing, observed, lower, upper, warmup = 24 * 90,
                         objective = "nse", start = "soil", control = list(maxit = 60))
fit_bc <- calibrate_pdm(start, forcing, observed, lower, upper, warmup = 24 * 90,
                        objective = "boxcox", start = "soil", control = list(maxit = 60))
rbind(truth = c(fc = 1, distribution.cmax = 300, surface.k1 = 2, distribution.b = 0.4),
      nse = fit_nse$parameters, boxcox = fit_bc$parameters)
```

Both come close here, but the Box-Cox calibration comes closer on the soil store (`cmax` 302 mm
against 305, `b` 0.40 against 0.42, the truth 300 and 0.40): NSE is pulled by the few peaks,
the Box-Cox objective by the record as a whole. Where some flows are measured worse than others, `flow_weights()`
turns a rating's uncertainty into weights, so flows above the highest gauging, on the
extrapolated part of the rating, count for less:

```{r weights, eval=FALSE}
w <- flow_weights(observed, highest_gauged = 12)
calibrate_pdm(start, forcing, observed, lower, upper, objective = "boxcox", weights = w)
```

# 2. Fit only what the record can pin down

Calibrations that disagree with each other are often fitting a parameter the record cannot
determine: many values fit equally well, and each search stops somewhere different.
`pdm_sensitivity()` finds such parameters across their whole range, with the others varying
too. Morris screening costs a few model runs per parameter.

```{r sensitivity, fig.height=3.6}
sens <- pdm_sensitivity(truth, forcing, observed, lower, upper,
                        objectives = c("nse_loss", "boxcox_loss"), r = 12, warmup = 24 * 90,
                        start = "soil")
sens
plot(sens)
```

`mu_star` is how much the score moves when a parameter does; `sigma` how much that depends on
the others. Here all four parameters matter and none is marked negligible: a short list chosen
with care. With the dozen or so parameters of a richer structure, those marked negligible can
be fixed at a regional or default value: the calibration then searches only what the data can
find, and repeated calibrations agree. For a
finer answer, `method = "sobol"` apportions the score's variance between the parameters, at the
cost of a few thousand runs.

# 3. Judge a forecasting model by its forecasts

A model's job is to forecast a few hours ahead with updating, not to reproduce a record.
`compare_forecasts()` hindcasts candidates alike and ranks them by skill over persistence at
the lead times that matter.

```{r forecasts}
cmp <- compare_forecasts(list(nse = fit_nse$model, boxcox = fit_bc$model), forcing, observed,
                         horizon_h = 12, every_h = 12, ar = list(), leads_h = c(1, 3, 6))
cmp$ranking
```

Here the two are all but equal as forecasters, 0.868 against 0.868: with updating, the small
differences in their parameters wash out within hours. That is worth knowing before arguing
over which is better. With `thresholds`, and `rank_on = "threshold"`, they are ranked by how
well they warn instead.

# 4. Will it hold in a different climate?

A model calibrated on wet years may fail in a drought, and the reverse. `split_sample_test()`
calibrates on the drier half of the years and scores the wetter half, then the reverse.

```{r split}
sst <- split_sample_test(start, forcing, observed, lower, upper, objective = "boxcox",
                         start = "soil", control = list(maxit = 40))
sst$scores[, c("calibrated_on", "scored_on", "nse", "boxcox_nse", "volume_error")]
```

A score that holds from dry to wet, here, means the calibration does not lean on the
conditions it was fitted in. `parameter_drift()` calibrates each period of the record on its
own: parameters that wander from period to period, steadily, point to a change in the
catchment or the record that one long calibration would average away.

# 5. How sure are we?

`calibrate_bayes()` returns not one set but a sample of every set consistent with the record
and with what was known beforehand (the priors), in proportion to how well each fits. The
spread is the parameters' uncertainty. A prior can come from a model of parameters from
catchment descriptors (`priors_from_table()`); here it is a loose one on `fc`.

```{r bayes}
post <- calibrate_bayes(truth, forcing, observed, lower = lower[1:2], upper = upper[1:2],
                        priors = list(fc = prior_normal(1, 0.3)), generations = 800,
                        lambda = 0, warmup = 24 * 90, start = "soil", seed = 3)
post
```

The likelihood behind it treats the errors on Box-Cox flows as running on from one hour to the
next, a lag-1 autoregression. Treating hourly errors as independent would make the posterior far
too sure of itself. R-hat under about 1.2 says the chains agree; a trial with 300 generations
stayed above it, so this run uses 800. The errors in this record are proportional to the flow, so the
power of the transform is 0 (the log); a real record's power is a choice to check, as section 6
shows.

Even so, three years of hourly flow pin `fc` down to within a fraction of a per cent. The
posterior is honest about the parameters given this model and these data; it says nothing about
errors in the rain, which calibrating on the rainfall used operationally deals with. Where it is still too sure, `temper` below 1 counts the record as worth less.

`posterior_band()` runs sets drawn from the posterior. Without the error model the band is the
parameters' uncertainty alone; with it, the band is what the observed flow should scatter in.

```{r band}
band <- posterior_band(post, forcing, draws = 50, noise = TRUE)
rows <- which.max(observed) + seq(-72, 120)
plot(forcing$time[rows], observed[rows], type = "l", xlab = "", ylab = "Flow (m3/s)",
     main = "The largest flood, with the 90% predictive band")
polygon(c(forcing$time[rows], rev(forcing$time[rows])), c(band$q05[rows], rev(band$q95[rows])),
        col = grDevices::adjustcolor("#0072B2", 0.25), border = NA)
lines(forcing$time[rows], band$q50[rows], col = "#0072B2", lwd = 1.5)
```

# 6. Is a probability forecast honest?

An ensemble says how likely a threshold is to be crossed. `ensemble_scores()` checks whether it
means what it says: the CRPS (the whole distribution against what happened), the spread against
the error (near 1 when the ensemble is as wide as its errors), Brier scores for thresholds, and
rank histograms. Here, the posterior runs with and without the error model, used as ensembles
of the observed flow:

```{r ensembles}
draws <- function(noise) {
  b <- vapply(1:20, function(i) posterior_band(post, forcing, draws = 1, probs = 0.5,
                                               noise = noise, seed = i)$q50,
              numeric(nrow(forcing)))
  b[seq(24 * 90, nrow(forcing), by = 6), ]
}
y <- observed[seq(24 * 90, nrow(forcing), by = 6)]
high <- c(high = unname(stats::quantile(observed, 0.98)))
rbind(parameters_only = ensemble_scores(draws(FALSE), y, thresholds = high),
      with_errors = ensemble_scores(draws(TRUE), y, thresholds = high))[
  , c("crps", "spread_skill", "brier:high")]
```

The parameters alone give an ensemble far narrower than its errors: a spread-skill ratio well
below 1, claiming far more certainty than it has. With the error model the ensemble is about as
wide as its errors, the ratio near 1, and its CRPS and Brier score are better too.

The power of the transform matters here. The same calibration with `lambda = 0.5` gives a ratio
of about 0.6: on that scale the errors of the highest flows look smaller than they are, so the
ensemble is too narrow exactly where it matters. The spread-skill ratio and the rank histogram
are how to tell. The same scores, by lead time, judge a real ensemble forecast.

# In short

| Question | Function |
|---|---|
| Are all the errors counted fairly? | `objective = "boxcox"`, `flow_weights()` |
| Which parameters can the record determine? | `pdm_sensitivity()` |
| Which model forecasts best? | `compare_forecasts()` |
| Will it hold in another climate? | `split_sample_test()`, `parameter_drift()` |
| How sure are we of it? | `calibrate_bayes()`, `posterior_band()` |
| Is a probability forecast honest? | `ensemble_scores()`, `crps_ensemble()`, `brier_score()` |
